utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning to the legal officers, the court reporters, the registrar; good morning, Ms. Hollis, Mr. Waidyaratne; good morning, Defence counsel. I think they are all present. Good morning, the accused. I should like us to go into closed session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we can have the witness brought in, please, Mr. Usher, so that we can continue with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nusret Sivac. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to remind you that you are continuing to testify under oath, and you will be answering questions put to you by Ms. Hollis. Ms. Hollis, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you testified about an incident in the garage when a person you knew by the nickname Zuti took Muhamed Cehajic from the garage. This nickname Zuti, were any other guards in the camp known by this nickname?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how many other guards were known by this nickname?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew Zeljko Marmat under this nickname, because we called him Zuti as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And could you describe this Zeljko Marmat for the Court?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Marmat, I think, was one of the worst guards, and as far as I can recollect, he was in Ckalja's shift. He was dressed most frequently, because sometimes they would change their clothing, in a blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd now like to ask you about several incidents, beginning with incidents that occurred while you were on the pista at Omarska. Before being taken to Omarska, did you know a man named Rizo Hadzalic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rizo Hadzalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know what his occupation was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a worker in a metalworking company called Bosna Montaza.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did you know a man named Kardum before being taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While on the pista do you recall an incident involving both Rizo and Kardum?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in what month did that incident occur?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sometime in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And by your estimate, how many detainees were being held on the pista at the time of this incident?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very many. I think around 500, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, on this occasion, before the incident involving Rizo and Kardum, did you see other detainees being abused?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day, all the detainees taken for interrogation would first be taken in front of the entrance outside the stairwell leading upstairs to the interrogation rooms, and there all those who were taken for interrogation were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And would you please tell the Judges what you saw of the incident involving Rizo and Kardum?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before they came, we were told that we could get up, because we spent most of our time with our heads bowed and looking at the ground. Somebody said, "They're taking Rizo and Gogi, at the pista," and we all looked, and indeed I think among the detainees that had been called out for interrogation were Rizo Hadzalic and Goran Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to Gogi, to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to Goran Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what did you see then after you had seen that they had been called out?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to the entrance near those pillars leading to the administration building itself. We looked, and for a moment they stopped, and they exchanged a few words with the guards. They talked to the guards. Shortly after that, I don't know how long after, we saw the guards who had been standing next to those pillars. I think they were Paspalj and Savic, were yelling very loudly at Rizo and Goran and beating them. We saw guards running from other guard posts to the spot where the incident was taking place. Then we heard a loud order telling us to lie down, which meant we had to face the asphalt face down. Terrible cries and moans were heard. I had the feeling as if somebody was breaking up the asphalt we were lying on. I don't know how long this went on for. Then those cries subsided a little, shouts were heard by the guards, "To the end, to the bitter end. Turks, this is how all of you will fare." We lay there, face down on the ground, and this lasted for some time actually. After a little time, a voice was heard of one of the guards. I didn't see who it was because I was lying face down when he said, "I need two strong guys." He picked two of the detainees over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that before you were told to lie face down, you saw guards running from other areas. Did you recognise any of the guards that were running toward this area where Rizo and Kardum were?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised Pop and Sole, who were running from this side, from the right-hand side, from the right of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if the witness could please be provided with Exhibit 3/112.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at that exhibit, and if you could point to the area where Rizo and Kardum were taken?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this spot here. There's this wall left of the pillars.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So these are the pillars that hold up this canopy over the entry to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were brought to the left, here against this wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that the two guards, you thought Paspalj and Sole were there. Could you show the Judges where those two guards were?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were next to these pillars.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you also indicated that when you saw the other guards running toward this area, that you saw a guard, but with the nickname Pop. Where did you see him coming from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and Sole were here somewhere, and they ran this way to the spot where the incident was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So as you look at the photo, they would have been coming from the corner of the building on the right, moving past the circular staircase.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Q.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You can leave that there, but I won't need your assistance for the moment, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you eventually allowed to change from your face-down position?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of the shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, after this occasion, did you yourself ever see Rizo or Kardum again?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just heard from the detainees, who were in this spot on the pista -- may I show you? -- that these two strong detainees called out by the guard dragged Rizo here to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you are showing an area of the pista as we look at the photograph close to those two pillars but to the left?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, this day, during this incident with Rizo and before that when you saw these other people beaten, did you see any of the shift commanders or camp leaders present?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frequently in this glassed-in area, Mladjo Radic, shift leader, would be standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You're talking about this day with this incident with Rizo and Kardum and the other people beaten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw him standing in this circular stairway by the window above A21, what would he be doing when you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably overseeing the guards, to see how they were treating the detainees that were being brought there and taken for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that day, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What weapons, if any, did he have?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always carried his rifle, an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you testified on that day that he was wearing a blue police uniform. What did he normally wear when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He most frequently wore a blue police uniform and sometimes he would have a beret on his head.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to Mladjo Radic, did you see any other camp leaders on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were sitting normally, I noticed that here, in this glassed-in area, Drago Prcac appeared a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, you were pointing to the glass area of the stairwell?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, these occasions that you saw Drago Prcac appear on that day, were prisoners being beaten at the times that you saw him at that glass area?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually when these detainees began to be beaten, we were ordered to lie down face down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So at the time you saw him, nobody was being beaten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think at that moment they were going for fresh detainees who were being prepared for the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention to another incident while you were on the pista. Do you recall a day when all detainees were beaten as they went to their meal?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did these beatings go on?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beating started as soon as the first groups were taken to the meal, and it lasted throughout the meal-taking period, from 9.00 a.m. until 3.00 in the afternoon, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was done to the detainees on this day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the groups that went to the meal on that day had to pass a gauntlet, that is, two lines of guards who were standing here in this area and who were beating the detainees on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this gauntlet, was it outside the building or inside the building or both?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the guards were standing outside near the pillars, and the other part was standing inside, in the corridor leading to the restaurant area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, while these beatings were going on, did you see any of the camp leadership?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, in this glass area here, during the day, that is, while we were beaten, almost all of them came, the guards, the investigators, together with their assistants, typists, and all other people who were doing administrative work. They were here in this glass area. They would come and go, but there would always be somebody standing there, cynically laughing at what was happening to us downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, again you were pointing to the window area of the circular staircase; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of some of the people that would come and watch what was happening and laugh?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall those merry faces very well of Zeljko Meakic, Dragan Radakovic, Drago Prcac, Slavica Lakic, Nada Markovska, Drago Meakic, Obrad Despotovic, Ilija Bjelic. They all used to be my colleagues at work, and I knew them very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the people that you have mentioned, including Obradic --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrad Despotovic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Bjelic. What did those people do in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the investigators in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic, to your knowledge, what was his position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the chief commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On this day did you see any of the shift commanders present at these beatings?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mladjo Radic was the shift leader on that day, Mladjo Radic, Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were being taken from the pista to the restaurant and as we were being lined up, he was standing at the beginning of the gauntlet. As the group was entering the restaurant, he would announce to the guards who were in the corridor that a new group was coming, a new group of detainees, and that they should get ready for beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, did you see Mladjo Radic himself beat any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe as you were pointing to the exhibit, you were pointing to the area around those two pillars at the entrance to the administration building. That's where the gauntlet began; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness could please be provided with Exhibit 3/77A.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that that gauntlet was also inside the restaurant building. Could you show us where?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the area marked as A13. Here at the beginning, across from rooms number A15 and A16.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you yourself have to run the gauntlet that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see Mladjo Radic inside the building in that area you have just pointed to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When my group had finished with the meal, before we came back, we had to line up in the area marked as A22, in this part here. I was at the front, I was ahead, and I was waiting for Mladjo Radic, who was at the beginning of the gauntlet but this time inside, I was waiting for him to give us the sign to move on toward the exit. Meanwhile, in this area which we had to pass through, the guards started putting various kinds of obstacles, pieces of furniture. They spilled some greasy liquid on the floor as well so as to make our exit even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So they put these objects and this grease in this corridor marked A13?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then, sir, what happened when you had to exit along that corridor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we reached the gauntlet, Mladjo Radic gave a sign for the beating to begin. I was the first one to pass through the gauntlet, and it is true Mladjo Radic didn't hit me at all, but others did. And the same happened to the detainees who were running behind me. I could hear them moan and scream, and I could hear blows, and all other noises that accompany beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you got outside, what happened to you outside? Blank page inserted o ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were here in this area behind the pillar, near the exit, a guard came out whose surname was Savic -- he was wearing a light blue shirt at the time -- and he landed a very heavy blow on me. He used a kind of a whip which had a ball on one of its ends, and he hit me with it on my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What injuries did you suffer as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I thought that half of my head was missing. I couldn't see anything on my right eye, and my friends from the pista told me that I had fallen outside the stairwell and that they had to drag me to the pista. I remember very well when I came to I saw Mustafa Muhic standing above me together with Dr. Esad Sadikovic. I couldn't see anything on my right eye, and my head was swollen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Those exhibit can be removed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Asmir Crnalic before being taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were born and we lived for a very long time on the same street in Prijedor, Muharema Suljanovica street.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he have any nicknames that he was known by?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well when, we were children we called him Ico.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So his nickname was Ico?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Vico, with a V.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And were there any other nicknames by which he was known?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had quite a few nicknames later on. Kera was one of them. He was a very nice young man. People liked him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident involving him while you were on the pista?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court what it is you personally saw or heard during that incident.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the hottest day of our stay in the Omarska camp. I remember that even the asphalt was melting because of very high temperatures. We didn't have enough water. We would receive water only from time to time. It was in the afternoon, we were sitting normally, we were not in the face-down position, and at one point one could hear some noise coming from the first row. When we looked that way, we saw -- I saw Asmir Crnalic, Vico, getting up. He was in one of the first rows. And he got up without permission of the guard. He started to act in a strange way. He started to dance, to make some kind of ballet movements, pirouettes. He was in the area between the detainees who were on the pista and the guards who were standing in the entrance to the administration building. He held a kind of bottle in his hand, and he was trying to drink from that bottle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see after that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, the guards were just laughing and inciting him, telling him to do some more, and Vico seemed to have accepted the game. But then at one point, one of the guards came and stopped his show, and he took him to the "white house." We could see that quite clearly, because at that moment we were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten minutes later, perhaps not even that long, an order could be heard telling us to lie down. So we all lie down in the face-down position, and then we heard a burst of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to this burst of gunfire, what else, if anything, did you hear?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard shouts, the usual shouts uttered by the guards, "Grab him. Finish him off to the end."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what happened after you heard the gunfire? What did you personally see or hear?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. For a while there was silence. This lasted for some time. When we were allowed to get up -- and in the meantime, the shift had changed, and the detainees who were on the left side of the pista told us that Vico had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now -- I'm sorry, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asmir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were allowed to get up, then what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ckalja, the shift leader, appeared, and he asked if anyone knew the guy. I said I knew him very well, and I told him his name. Then Ckalja took a piece of paper and wrote down the name, and he took it to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you told him the name of this person, how far away from the person were you, from this person you identified as Vico?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ckalja, since he had told me to approach him, I changed my position. If I can show it to you on the map. Maybe 20 or 30 metres away. I could recognise Vico who was lying outside the "white house" in a strange position. He had his dirty white T-shirt on and a pair of jeans, but was wearing no shoes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown 3/104.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at that, are you able to tell the Court where you were when you spoke with Ckalja and where the body was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was standing here with Ckalja, on the right side of the restaurant, in this part of the pista, and Vico's body was in front of the "white house," to the left, near the path leading to the "white house," on the grass area in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So as we look at the photo of the "white house," it would be to the left the sidewalk, near the window on the left?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And where you had pointed to the pista on the photograph would have been an area just to the left of the top corner of the restaurant building pointing toward the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, I'd like to ask you about some incidents in Mujo's room. Did you know a person by the name of Zgog before you were brought to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Bajram Zgog, who was an Albanian by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And was he in Mujo's room with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was with us in Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident when he was beaten in that room by guards?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you recognise those guards who beat him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could. It was rather unusual for the guards Pop and Sole to come to Mujo's room and say that the coach, trainer, should come out. That was the nickname that they had given to him. But he remained silent for a while. But the detainees around him encouraged him to respond. However, he kept saying that he was not a coach, that he was a simple football player.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, so the guards actually came into the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They came to the area that I can show you, near the toilets, to the area which is facing the inside of -- the interior part of Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man by the name of Zijad Mahmuljin before being brought to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Zijad Mahmuljin is an economist, and he held a number of offices in the Prijedor municipality, and I think that before the war he was one of the managers of the D/P Jela company, wood processing -- it was a wood processing factory in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you also known a man by the name of Zlatan Besirevic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatan Besirevic was an engineer, and he was the manager of a metal factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man by the name Nedzad Seric?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his occupation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a lawyer by occupation, and he was the president of the Prijedor court for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were these men in Mujo's room with you as well?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the condition of these men when you saw them in Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in very bad, very poor condition. They were taken out on a number of occasions and beaten up. So you could see traces of terrible tortures and blows on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall today any of the shifts on which they were taken out and beaten?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken out on almost every shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall Mahmuljin and Besirevic being taken together from Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they first took Zlatan Besirevic out, and only later on in the evening hours Zijad Mahmuljin was taken as well. I think that the president of the municipality, Muhamed Cehajic, then Meho Kapetanovic, Ziko Crnaljic, a private caterer, Idriz Jakupovic, who was the manager of the social welfare centre, then another lawyer from the municipality were taken out on that same night.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, sir, after all these people were taken out, did you ever see them again?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Nedzad Seric, do you recall his being taken from the room?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when he was taken out at that time, do you recall if he came back to the room on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Nedzad Saric, he was taken out very often, and most of the time he was not able to come back to the room on his own. They would leave him at the entrance and then Burho or Mujo, who were some kind of leaders of our room, would go and help him back into the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, was there ever an occasion that he was taken from your room and did not return to your room?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was at the end of July, between the 25th and the 30th of July. They kept taking people out all the time, and I think that during that period of time, massive killings were committed. It was during that period of time that most of the people were taken out, most of them intellectuals and other prominent citizens of Prijedor, and they never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man by the name of Eso Mehmedagic before being taken to Omarksa?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see this man in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I knew Eso Mehmedagic for a long time and I saw him in the Omarska camp. He's a half-blind man.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was his condition when you saw him in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a very bad condition. As I told you, Eso Mehmedagic had very poor sight, and he lost his glasses in the Omarska camp and he couldn't move around. So he would usually be the last one in the groups running to the restaurant for a meal, and he would -- he would be holding the person in the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when you last saw him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that while I was on the pista at one occasion, he went for a meal. Eso Mehmedagic was actually in the hangar, so the only time I could see him was while I was on the pista. When I moved to Mujo's room, I didn't see him after that any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were on the pista, did you personally ever see Eso Mehmedagic being beaten or abused?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw it on that day when we were all beaten up while going for a meal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you taken from Omarska to Trnopolje on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. On the 6th of August in a group of 700 detainees, I was taken to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken to Omarska on the 20th of June or about the 23rd of June, excuse me, how would you describe your condition at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean my condition? I'm not quite sure I understand. You mean the difference between my condition when I arrived in Omarska and my condition when I left Omarska? You probably mean that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That would be helpful. Please tell the Judges that difference.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I entered Omarska, I was more or less completely healthy, well-fed person, and when I left Omarska I weighed 34 kilograms less than I did originally. I was in bad shape, and I could not see very well on my right eye.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in Prijedor until the 16th of December, 1992, when I managed to leave for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the conditions like for you in Prijedor when you went back to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us Bosniak Muslims and Croats, conditions were awful. The town was full of gangs out of control, Zoran Zigic, Dosen -- and they simply engaged in a headhunt.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, why did you decide to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all Bosniak Muslims, Croats, and the other non-Serbs, there was no life to lead in Prijedor any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you have to do in order to be allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I had to make a gift of all my property, movable and immovable to the Serb authorities, and to make all kinds of certificates, I had to give up all my savings which I had collected on the basis of my work, 30-year long career.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court the physical, emotional, and psychological impact on you of the abuse that you suffered in Omarska and the conditions there.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, after everything I lived through during the days I spent in those camps, it is not simple for me to tell you about it and I get very emotional because this was inflicted upon us by people I used to work with, and that is why my emotions gain control over me. Unfortunately, in those death camps, almost all Croats and Muslims who used to work with me in the security service were killed. The number of us that remain can be counted on the fingers of one hand. I think, Your Honours, all those who committed crimes will be brought to justice by this Tribunal and punished adequately. And I wish to draw your attention to the fact that one of those -- among those who are to blame are the men who are sitting here, but of course, you will judge that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the property --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could talk to you about the property that you had in 1992. Did you ever receive that property back?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. As far as I know, my weekend home and orchard, they have been destroyed. As for the apartment, it's probably inhabited by a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, sir, have you ever been paid for that property?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have testified about Kvocka, Prcac, Radic, and Kos. Sir, I would ask you to look around the courtroom and tell the Judges if you recognise the person Kvocka in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My former neighbour. He's sitting in the middle with headphones. Yes, they all have headphones. He has a dark jacket and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, sir, as you're looking toward that area, in what row is he seated?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The top row, just below the glass.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, sir, would you tell the Court if you recognise the man you knew as Radic, in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My former colleague, Mladjo Radic, Krkan, he is to the left of Kvocka as I am looking at them and to the right of Kvocka wearing a purple jacket and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And who is to the right of Mr. Kvocka as you view them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I am looking at them, an acquaintance of mine from the Omarska camp, Milojica Kos, known as Krle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And would you look around courtroom and tell Their Honours if you see the person you knew as Prcac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's here, right next to the policeman. He's writing something. In a brown jacket and tie, wearing glasses, and a moustache. In the Omarska camp, Prcac did not have a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would note positive identifications, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. I think perhaps before we begin with the cross-examination we should have a break, and I should like to ask the usher to see the witness out. We're going to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, what will be the order of the cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The order will be slightly changed. I will be cross-examining at the end. The rest will be according to the order in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Witness, you're now going to answer questions which Defence counsel have for you, and they will also introduce themselves. I see Mr. O'Sullivan. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Eugene O'Sullivan, and I'm a lawyer from Canada. You testified about the shooting of your friend, Mr. Asmir Crnalic, as Vico and Kera. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you knew him to be a mental patient, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on the pista when he stood up and asked for water, he was nervous and agitated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear him ask for water. I just saw him get up and start jumping around.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Was he given -- he was given a bottle of water by a prisoner, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was in the bottle, but I saw that he was drinking from a bottle.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at one point he began spitting water towards a guard?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He was taken to the "white house."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At one point you saw Mr. Crnalic jump from the window of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that, nor did I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then you say he was shot dead by a burst of gunfire from an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, while we were lying down, we were ordered to lie face down. At that moment we heard a burst of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you told Ckalja the name of the man who was shot?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After some time, when we were allowed to get up and when we were lining up to go to sleep in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Ckalja is the person known as Momo Gruban; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Momo Gruban wrote your name down when you gave him the name of Crnalic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He just wrote down the name of Asmir Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when this shooting occurred, Momo Gruban's guard shift was on duty, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was Krle's shift that was on duty then, Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Of the guards present, the one who fired the shots wore a hood and always manned a guard post between the "white house" and the pista; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that later from the women detainees among whom was my sister, and they were sitting in the restaurant and watching all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, could I ask that these documents be placed in front of the witness, and could you show them to the Prosecutor first. Now, sir, you have two documents in front of you. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One document is in English and one is a translation of the English document into Bosnian. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: They're both there because we work in three languages here, English, French, and your language. So we must work our way through this. All right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can you look at the front page of the Bosnian version, and there you see that that is the statement -- a witness statement made to the Tribunal in 1994, and your name appears on the front. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the English version, at the bottom right-hand corner of the English version you see your signature, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And keeping with the English version, if you flip through the English version, at the bottom right-hand corner of every page is your signature. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On all 36 pages you signed the bottom right corner; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Just take a moment. Do you see that you signed every page of that statement in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And before signing this statement, it was read back to you in Bosnian by the interpreter who was present during the interview; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And she read it back to you in your language before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you turn to the last page of the English version you'll see your signature and the date of the 16th of October, 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The front page of this statement indicates that you were interviewed from the 12th to the 16th of November, 1994. Does that seem correct to you? That's when this took place?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it is probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Does that mean that you met every day for five days with the investigators? Between the 12th and the 16th, did you meet every day? Do you recall meeting every day over those five days?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea of how many hours per day you met? Was it a full working day with normal breaks? Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly so. They worked at a very intensified pace, as far as I can remember. They even stayed until late into the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were interviewed by two people, based on what the cover page says. Is that how you remember it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you gave this statement voluntarily; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, voluntarily. What I knew at the time I told them about and what I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And no pressure was put on you to make a statement, was it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you spoke freely when you gave your answers and explanations?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you gave this statement approximately two years after the events of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years after?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In 1994, two years after the events of Omarska, approximately two years after.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And these events were fresher in your mind then than they are today?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much fresher.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you gave your best account and recollection of events, people, and places?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you told the truth?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I saw I told them about.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you told the truth?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the truth and only the truth, as one says.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I ask you it take the Bosnian version and turn to page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Those following in English, it's page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Have you found page 21?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to the top of the page, the first line. I'm going to read it to you. Please listen. "My friend Asmir Crnalic was lying on the pista. He was a mental patient. He needed some water so stood and demanded water. A couple of guards approached. Asmir was having a nervous attack and he was agitated. A prisoner gave him a small bottle of water, and he began spitting it towards the guards. They took him to the "white house." The "white house" had short walls with a large glass area so we could see clearly. Then we heard shouts and shooting. Vico, Asmir Crnalic, was trying to jump from the window. He did. He had lost control. He did jump down, and the guards shot him dead. The guard said he was shot trying to escape. Later, Momo joined his men. We were ordered to sit instead of lie down, and we were asked who knew Vico. I said I did, and Momo wrote my name and went back to his building. Weapon used was a Kragujevka auto-rifle fired in a burst. Of the guards present, the one who fired wore a hood and always manned a guard post between the "white house" and the pista." Let me direct your attention to one other passage on page 20 of the Bosnian version, sir. The previous page, at the bottom. I'm still on page 31 in English. I'll read it to you. In regards to this episode you said: "A couple of days later, another incident occurred on the pista. The shift leader was again Momo Gruban." Sir, were you telling the truth when you said this to investigators in 1994?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I never believed that I would be in the position of a witness in this way. I wanted to describe the situation we found ourselves in in the most graphic way, so it is quite possible that I made certain minor mistakes when it comes to details because a lot of time had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. elapsed in the meantime. However, as regards the very essence of it, I think that what I said on that occasion and what I'm telling today is almost the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that this statement was being taken and may be used for legal proceedings in this Tribunal, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what was explained to us at that time. It was indeed explained to us that the statement would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, could I direct your attention to the 20th of June, 1992. That was the time of your second arrest. You were arrested approximately on the 20th of June for the second time, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. I don't remember it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You were arrested on that day at about 11.00 in the morning by Bato Kovacevic; right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you and the other people you named yesterday ended up at the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at the police station, you and the people you named were beaten and bloodied; right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They beat us savagely.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And from the police station you were taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Omarska, you told us you lined up behind the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, alongside the glass wall on this side of the restaurant, looking towards the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Kos was present when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You were not beaten on this occasion when you arrived in Omarska, were you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received only a couple of blows, and then someone said -- our faces were turned to the window. Someone said that it was enough, that we received enough blows for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I direct are attention to page 17 of your Bosnian version of your statement. Page 17 of the Bosnian, page 25 of the English. Have you found page 17, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the middle of the page the following words appear: "20th of June I was rearrested. Around 11.00, Bato Kovacevic came to my home and told me to follow him." Now, on that same page, 17, the last paragraph, page 26 in English, the second paragraph, it states: "We arrived at Omarska, and we were lined up behind the restaurant. Again I could see people laying on the pista. We stood against the wall. The same shift leader as before said I was back and this time no mistake. This time we were not beaten, as we were covered in blood." Sir, you were telling the truth when you said this in 1994, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Compared to the beatings we sustained later on, this was still quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to June the 10th, the day of your first arrest. When you arrived in Omarska on June the 10th by van, who was in the van with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the van together with me, sitting at the back side, was Omer Kerenovic, Safet Ramadanovic, Ivica Muntijan, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but do you really need the witness to repeat what he has already said? He said that Safet Ramadanovic was with him in the van together with some other people. Do you really need to hear all that over again?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In his direct examination, he did not mention who was with him on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe he did indicate who was with him on the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have my notes here. He has indeed mentioned the individuals who were with him. Please try to streamline your questions, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So there were three of you in the van that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three people were there with me. I was the fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But when you left Omarska that day on June the 10th, you went home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first went to the police station in Prijedor, and I had to wait for a while for them to check what to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then you went home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went in the direction of the centre. I think I went home, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you visited your sister Nusreta that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember at this point but this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, my name is Toma Fila. I'm an attorney-at-law from Belgrade. Together with my colleague Mr. Jovanovic, I'm representing Mladjo Radic in this case. Could you please describe for us the SDS flag that you saw in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have described it already. You have probably received the description. I think it's the SDS flag. It has a cross with two letters "S" written in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it's a Serbian flag, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I have already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Because I have never heard of an SDS flag.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know when exactly the shifts would be rotated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour, but counsel is, in effect, testifying on the record. We would ask that he restrict himself to questions. When he's saying that he's never heard of an SDS flag, that in fact it's a Serbian flag, what's really happening is that counsel is attempting to put evidence on the record. We would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know what time of day it was when the shifts would be rotated and how was it organised?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be rotated every 12 hours, at 7.00 a.m. and at 7.00 p.m. again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not familiar with the procedure itself. However, at the end of our stay in the camp, when we were allowed outside Mujo's room and when we could move relatively freely near the water taps, we could see that near the flag, on an asphalt area, guards would be lined up, the guards who were supposed to take over the duty. First the guards who were take over the duty would come there, and then from the guard posts, the guards leaving duty would come to the same spot. However, it is very important to say that many of the guards in the camp would come not only by buses but also by their own private tractors, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I simply wanted to know the procedure, so that would be enough. Thank you, Witness. The people who were in charge of interrogations on the first floor of the administration building and whose names you have mentioned as names of the people who used to be your colleagues were actually interrogators?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were professionals, that is, workers who used to work at the public security service, people who were with the police, but there were also certain individuals who were from other branches. There was a professor there whose name was Miroslav Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude or do you perhaps know the hierarchy? Who was superior to whom?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the investigators, to the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. I want to know whether the interrogators were superior to Mladjo Radic or the other way around.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interrogators were doing their job. All the information they gathered would be then provided to Ranko Mijic, who was their chief, and he would probably leave the appropriate instructions to the shift leaders so that they could do their job during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question to you, Witness, was very simple. Who was able to issue orders to whom? Was Ranko Mijic issuing records to Mladjo Radic or the other way around?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interrogators themselves were able to order things to the guards, and especially, in particular, Ranko Mijic, who was their chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We can, therefore, conclude that they were superior to Mladjo Radic, that they could issue orders to him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. Fila, but there is one thing you should know, if I may, that the shift leaders and many of the guards did things on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that people would be called out and then taken away or would go by themselves to see the interrogators on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They never went on their own. A guard would always come to pick them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to discuss the procedure. How did it go?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually where a guard would come, he would come to the room where the person who was supposed to be interrogated was, he would ask whether the individual in question was there, and very often the people who were supposed to be taken out were not in that room but happened to find themselves in some other room.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. And then the guard would take him where exactly?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the guard would take him away. However, there were people who were especially in charge of bringing people for interrogation, and the guard would take the individual in question through the stairwell to the offices upstairs. And at the beginning of the corridor there was a small desk, and Rade Knezevic who was a retired investigator would sit at that desk. He had a very big book, and he would record the names of the detainees who were supposed to be interrogated in that room, and he was the one who would indicate the room where they were supposed to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the role of the guard would finish at that point, when the individual was brought to Ranko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He would enter the room where the individual in question was supposed to be interrogated, and then, upon request of one of the interrogators, he would actually enter the room. Sometimes he would bring even more guards and they would all be present at the interrogation of the detainee.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So once the interrogation was over?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the detainee was still able to walk, then together with the people who had brought him there, he would leave the room and go back to the area indicated. However, if he was unable to walk alone, then two people from the pista would be called to pick him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, conclude that whatever happened to the individual in question would happen in the room during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spoke about an incident involving a person by the name of Smail, who was thrown into a truck tyre. You said that the incident took place in the afternoon hours. You spoke about that during your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smail Duratovic you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us the time of the day when the tyre was on fire? Could you tell us approximately what time it was and what shift was on duty?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the time of day was. All I know was that it took place in the afternoon hours and that Smail Duratovic was recognised while he was going for lunch. He was taken by one of the guards, but I cannot tell you the details because I was not looking while he was being thrown into the tyre, but this took place before his return to Mujo's room. That is when we learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it during the lunchtime?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was during the afternoon hours. And Smail Duratovic, I think, spent one night in the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You wouldn't know the shift that was on duty at the time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did the guards have?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right at this start, I have to say that I'm by no means an expert in weapons. I don't like those toys. But they had various kinds of weapons, as far as I could observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that Mladjo Radic had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did other guards have the same rifle?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us now move to the incident that took place in the restaurant, when this greasy liquid was spilled on the floor. Was that liquid thrown on the floor while you were there or had it been thrown before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the liquid had been spilled before our arrival. However, due to numerous passages of various groups, the whole floor was covered in that liquid, and they would have to renew the process with each passing group.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This is what they put at the very entrance. They put some pieces of furniture there, parts of tables, chairs, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How much time did you have to enter the room, to eat, and to leave the room? Did you enter the room running?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did. We had to run very fast, and our lunches -- that was the shortest lunch we ever had. We didn't even have enough time to eat, we just took a piece of bread. We didn't even have time to take the plates. And then we went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you were at the front part of your group of people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well that Marijan Zec, an economist from Prijedor, was behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you had to run back to the exit?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how long were you able to observe Mladjo Radic while you were running?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had enough time because we had been lined up against the glass wall. So I had to look inside waiting for the sign so that we can start getting out, because we couldn't get out on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And as you were getting out, you had to run?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We had to run up to the obstacles that had been set up in front of us, and that is when the trouble began.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you said that he did not hit you. You simply passed him by.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What else could you see?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could hear moans, screams. I could hear people falling down, people being kicked away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you saw?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see the guards who were ready, waiting for us in that area. They were waiting for us with their clubs, baseball bats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But Mladjo Radic was not with them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. And then this terrible incident happened to you.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. During that incident, you were on the pista or in Mujo's room? I mean, during the night.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were on the pista, but during the night we would enter the restaurant area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have only one other question for you, Witness. You stated that you knew Mladjo Radic before this quite regrettable events.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where exactly did you work together? You were a member of a public security service and he was a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the public security service. It is a very complex organisation but it's surprising that you are not familiar with it. I was not a member of the police. My service, the communication service, through various organisational changes, changed authority. We were part of the public security service for a while and then we would shift. You know, exactly what happened to Rankovic in the former Yugoslavia. The communications service and the cryptoprotection service, at one point, were made part of the public security service. Which means, that they were only in charge to provide services to the public security service. However, all the powers were handed over to us and all the duties and assignments were handed over to us by the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. But I wanted to know where exactly it was when you worked with Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was an employee of that service, my main duty was to receive various written memoranda or messages which we then transmitted to various public security stations throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia. Mladjo Radic was an employee of a public security station, and very often he would bring a number these memoranda or messages which we then had to transmit elsewhere. So this is what we did while he was in the Ljubija police station and in the Kozarac public station, and also while he was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was it? In what year was that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think that Mladjo Radic went through all of the police stations in the area of Prijedor, but I couldn't tell you the exact date or time. I know that he would come to me, to my technical service, very often while he was working in Omarksa. So during that period of time, he would come is to see me very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That concludes my cross-examination of the witness, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Tosic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our team will not cross-examine this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Jovan Simic is next. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovan Simic, I'm an attorney from Belgrade and together with my colleague Mr. Masic. We represented Mr. Prcac. Did you know Mr. Prcac privately?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only from work. I mean, we didn't socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did -- was Mr. Prcac working in the Prijedor police station and what kind of work did he do?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before me, he came, I don't know how long before me. As far as I know, he came from Istria. I think he worked in Labin or Porec or somewhere as an ordinarily policeman. But when he came to the Prijedor SUP, he attended a course for crime technicians, I think somewhere in Sarajevo. He completed that course, and then he worked in the service department as a crime technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you engaged in similar or identical activities?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, our activities had very little in common, one could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you explain then where you were engaged together?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequently, upon returning from an inquest after a traffic accident or criminal offences that had been carried out, that Dragoljub Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prcac had to go and be present at, he had to submit a report about it with an official report addressed to his superior. And on the basis of that official report, he had to type out a telegram, a cable, and all this depended on the kind of offence or crime that had been committed. And depending on that, a different person had to be reported to. We, or rather, my security service, had to report to the centre of the security service in Banja Luka or the republican SUP in Sarajevo about all serious offences. He would bring those cables to me and we would forward them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were those cables brought to you by Drago or his superior?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Prcac would bring them very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Drago's responsibilities were prior to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Drago Prcac retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know when?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it was in the 1980s, but let me try and pinpoint it. I think it was in 1986, 1987, 1988. I may be wrong. I know that he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: So Prcac was retired?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were both members of the party, if that is of any interest to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, when the feature on Omarksa was filmed.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is interesting to note that my former colleagues who used to work for the Serb television came very frequently, and after the conflict --

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you a simple question. When was that feature filmed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Djukanovic and Dragoljub Prcac --
